entries.defb92a51d519d0a580518a5c201eaeeed8adb39: <div sID="gen17498" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="14" osisID="Jer.14" sID="Jer.14"/> <div eID="gen17498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17499" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17500" type="x-p"/> This chapter was penned upon occasion of a great drought, for want of rain. This judgment began in the latter end of Josiah's reign, but, as it should seem, continued in the beginning of Jehoiakim's: for less judgments are sent to give warning of greater coming, if not prevented by repentance. This calamity was mentioned several times before, but here, in this chapter, more fully. Here is, I. A melancholy description of it, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1-Jer.14.6">ver. 1-6</reference>. II. A prayer to God to put an end to this calamity and to return in mercy to their land, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.7-Jer.14.9">ver. 7-9</reference>. III. A severe threatening that God would proceed in his controversy, because they proceeded in their iniquity, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.10-Jer.14.12">ver. 10-12</reference>. IV. The prophet's excusing the people, by laying the blame on their false prophets; and the doom passed both on the deceivers and the deceived, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13-Jer.14.16">ver. 13-16</reference>. V. Directions given to the prophet, instead of interceding for them, to lament them; but his continuing notwithstanding to intercede for them, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.17-Jer.14.22">ver. 17-22</reference>.
entries.5b40864ae1584318563a54e3e01155f3b0d4a4c2: <div eID="gen17500" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17499" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Lamentation Caused by a Great Drought; Prayer for Mercy; Pleading with God. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi>  606.)</title> <div sID="gen17501" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> The word of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> that came to Jeremiah concerning the dearth. <hi type="super">2</hi> Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish; they are black unto the ground; and the cry of Jerusalem is gone up. <hi type="super">3</hi> And their nobles have sent their little ones to the waters: they came to the pits, <hi type="italic">and</hi> found no water; they returned with their vessels empty; they were ashamed and confounded, and covered their heads. <hi type="super">4</hi> Because the ground is chapt, for there was no rain in the earth, the plowmen were ashamed, they covered their heads. <hi type="super">5</hi> Yea, the hind also calved in the field, and forsook <hi type="italic">it,</hi> because there was no grass. <hi type="super">6</hi> And the wild asses did stand in the high places, they snuffed up the wind like dragons; their eyes did fail, because <hi type="italic">there was</hi> no grass. <hi type="super">7</hi> <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , though our iniquities testify against us, do thou <hi type="italic">it</hi> for thy name's sake: for our backslidings are many; we have sinned against thee. <hi type="super">8</hi> O the hope of Israel, the saviour thereof in time of trouble, why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land, and as a wayfaring man <hi type="italic">that</hi> turneth aside to tarry for a night? <hi type="super">9</hi> Why shouldest thou be as a man astonied, as a mighty man <hi type="italic">that</hi> cannot save? yet thou, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">art</hi> in the midst of us, and we are called by thy name; leave us not. <div eID="gen17501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17502" type="x-p"/> The first verse is the title of the whole chapter: it does indeed all <hi type="italic">concern the dearth,</hi> but much of it consists of the prophet's prayers concerning it; yet these are not unfitly said to be, <hi type="italic">The word of the Lord which came to him</hi> concerning it, for every acceptable prayer is that which God puts into our hearts; nothing is our word that comes to him but what is first his word that comes from him. In these verses we have, <div eID="gen17502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17503" type="x-p"/> I. The language of nature lamenting the calamity. When the heavens were as brass, and distilled no dews, the earth was as iron, and produced no fruits; and then the grief and confusion were universal. 1. The people of the land were all in tears. Destroy their vines and their fig-trees and you cause all their mirth to cease, <reference osisRef="Hos.2.11-Hos.2.12">Hos. ii. 11, 12</reference>. All their joy fails with the joy of harvest, with that of their corn and wine. <hi type="italic">Judah mourns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.2">v. 2</reference>), not for the sin, but for the trouble—for the withholding of the rain, not for the withdrawing of God's favour. <hi type="italic">The gates thereof,</hi> all that go in and out at their gates, <hi type="italic">languish,</hi> look pale, and grow feeble, for want of the necessary supports of life and for fear of the further fatal consequences of this judgment. <hi type="italic">The gates,</hi> through which supplies of corn formerly used to be brought into their cities, now look melancholy, when, instead of that, the inhabitants are departing through them to seek for bread in other countries. Even those that sit in the gates languish; <hi type="italic">they are black unto the ground,</hi> they go in black as mourners and sit on the ground, as the poor beggars at the gates are <hi type="italic">black in the face</hi> for want of food, <hi type="italic">blacker than a coal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lam.4.8">Lam. iv. 8</reference>. Famine is represented by a black horse, <reference osisRef="Rev.6.5">Rev. vi. 5</reference>. They fall to the ground through weakness, not being able to go along the streets. <hi type="italic">The cry of Jerusalem has gone up;</hi> that is, of the citizens (for the city is <hi type="italic">served by the field</hi>), or of people from all parts of the country met at Jerusalem to pray for rain; so some. But I fear it was rather the cry of their trouble, and the cry of their prayer. 2. The great men of the land felt from this judgment (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">The nobles sent their little ones to the water,</hi> perhaps their own children, having been forced to part with their servants because they had not wherewithal to keep them, and being willing to train up their children, when they were little, to labour, especially in a case of necessity, as this was. We find Ahab and Obadiah, the king and the lord chamberlain of his household, in their own persons, seeking for water in such a time of distress as this was, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.5-1Kgs.18.6">1 Kings xviii. 5, 6</reference>. Or, rather, <hi type="italic">their meaner ones,</hi> their servants and inferior officers; these they sent to seek for water, which there is no living without; but there was none to be found: They <hi type="italic">returned with their vessels empty;</hi> the springs were dried up when there was no rain to feed them; and then <hi type="italic">they</hi> (their masters that sent them) <hi type="italic">were ashamed and confounded</hi> at the disappointment. They would not be ashamed of their sins, nor confounded at the sense of them, but were unhumbled under the reproofs of the word, thinking their wealth and dignity set them above repentance; but God took a course to make them ashamed of that which they were so proud of, when they found that even on this side hell their nobility would not purchase them a drop of water to cool their tongue. Let our reading the account of this calamity make us thankful for the mercy of water, that we may not by the feeling of the calamity be taught to value it. What is most needful is most plentiful. 3. The husbandmen felt most sensibly and immediately from it (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">v. 4</reference>): <hi type="italic">The ploughmen were ashamed,</hi> for the ground was so parched and hard that it would not admit the plough even when it was so <hi type="italic">chapt</hi> and cleft that it seemed as if it did not need the plough. They were ashamed to be idle, for there was nothing to be done, and therefore nothing to be expected. The <hi type="italic">sluggard, that will not plough by reason of cold,</hi> is not ashamed of his own folly; but the diligent husbandman, that cannot plough by reason of heat, is ashamed of his own affliction. See what an immediate dependence husbandmen have upon the divine Providence, which therefore they should always have an eye to, for they cannot plough nor sow in hope unless God <hi type="italic">water their furrows,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.10">Ps. lxv. 10</reference>. 4. The case even of the wild beasts was very pitiable, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.5-Jer.14.6">v. 5, 6</reference>. Man's sin brings those judgments upon the earth which make even the inferior creatures groan: and the prophet takes notice of this as a plea with God for mercy. Judah and Jerusalem have sinned, but the hinds and the wild asses, what have they done? The hinds are pleasant creatures, lovely and loving, and particularly tender of their young; and yet such is the extremity of the case that, contrary to the instinct of their nature, they leave their young, even when they are newly calved and most need them, to seek for grass elsewhere; and, if they can find none, they <hi type="italic">abandon</hi> them, because not able to suckle them. It grieved not the hind so much that she had no grass herself as that she had none for her young, which will shame those who spend that upon their lusts which they should preserve for their families. The hind, when she has brought forth her young, is said to have <hi type="italic">cast forth her sorrows</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.39.3">Job xxxix. 3</reference>), and yet she continues her cares; but, as it follows there, she soon sees the good effect of them, for <hi type="italic">her young ones</hi> in a little while <hi type="italic">grow up,</hi> and trouble her no more, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">v. 4</reference>. But here the great trouble of all is that she has nothing for them. Nay, one would be sorry even for the <hi type="italic">wild asses</hi> (though they are creatures that none have any great affection for); for, though the <hi type="italic">barren land</hi> is made <hi type="italic">their dwelling</hi> at the best (<reference osisRef="Job.39.5-Job.39.6">Job xxxix. 5, 6</reference>), yet even that is now made too hot for them, so hot that they cannot breathe in it, but they get to the <hi type="italic">highest places</hi> they can reach, where the air is coolest, and <hi type="italic">snuff up the wind like dragons,</hi> like those creatures which, being very hot, are continually panting for breath. <hi type="italic">Their eyes fail,</hi> and so does their strength, <hi type="italic">because there is no grass</hi> to support them. The tame ass, that serves her owner, is welcome to <hi type="italic">his crib</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Isa. i. 3</reference>) and has her keeping for her labour, when the <hi type="italic">wild ass,</hi> that <hi type="italic">scorns the crying of the driver,</hi> is forced to <hi type="italic">live upon air,</hi> and is well enough served for not serving. <hi type="italic">He that will not labour, let him not eat.</hi> <div eID="gen17503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17504" type="x-p"/> II. Here is the language of grace, lamenting the iniquity, and complaining to God of the calamity. The people are not forward to pray, but the prophet here prays for them, and so excites them to pray for themselves, and puts words into their mouths, which they may make use of, in hopes to speed, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.7-Jer.14.9">v. 7-9</reference>. In this prayer, 1. Sin is humbly confessed. When we come to pray for the preventing or removing of any judgment we must always acknowledge that our <hi type="italic">iniquities testify against us.</hi> Our sins are witnesses against us, and true penitents see them to be such. They testify, for they are plain and evident; we cannot deny the charge. They testify against us, for our conviction, which tends to our present shame and confusion, and our future condemnation. They disprove and overthrow all our pleas for ourselves; and so not only accuse us, but answer against us. If we boast of our own excellencies, and trust to our own righteousness, our iniquities testify against us, and prove us perverse. If we quarrel with God as dealing unjustly or unkindly with us in afflicting us, our iniquities testify against us that we do him wrong; "for <hi type="italic">our backslidings are many</hi> and our revolts are great, whereby <hi type="italic">we have sinned against thee</hi>—too numerous to be concealed, for they are many, too heinous to be excused, for they are against thee." 2. Mercy is earnestly begged: "<hi type="italic">Though our iniquities testify against us,</hi> and against the granting of the favour which the necessity of our case calls for, yet <hi type="italic">do thou it.</hi>" They do not say particularly what they would have done; but, as becomes penitents and beggars, they refer the matter to God: "Do with us as thou thinkest fit," <reference osisRef="Judg.10.15">Judg. x. 15</reference>. Not, <hi type="italic">Do thou it</hi> in this way or at this time, but "<hi type="italic">Do thou it for thy name's sake;</hi> do that which will be most for the glory of thy name." Note, Our best pleas in prayer are those that are fetched from the glory of God's own name. "Lord, do it, that thy mercy may be magnified, thy promise fulfilled, and thy interest in the world kept up; we have nothing to plead in ourselves, but every thing in thee." There is another petition in this prayer, and it is a very modest one (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.9">v. 9</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Leave us not,</hi> withdraw not thy favour and presence." Note, We should dread and deprecate God's departure from us more than the removal of any or all our creature-comforts. 3. Their relation to God, their interest in him, and their expectations from him grounded thereupon, are most pathetically pleaded with him, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.8-Jer.14.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. (1.) They look upon him as one they have reason to think should deliver them when they are in distress, yea, though their iniquities testify against them; for in him mercy has often rejoiced against judgment. The prophet, like Moses of old, is willing to make the best he can of the case of his people, and therefore, though he must own that they have sinned many a great sin (<reference osisRef="Exod.32.31">Exod. xxxii. 31</reference>), yet he pleads, <hi type="italic">Thou art the hope of Israel.</hi> God has encouraged his people to hope in him; in calling himself so often the <hi type="italic">God of Israel,</hi> the <hi type="italic">rock of Israel,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">Holy One of Israel,</hi> he has made himself the <hi type="italic">hope of Israel.</hi> He has given Israel his word to hope in, and caused them to hope in it; and there are those yet in Israel that make God alone their hope, and expect he will be <hi type="italic">their Saviour in time of trouble,</hi> and they look not for salvation in any other; "Thou hast many a time been such, in the time of their extremity." Note, Since God is his people's all-sufficient Saviour, they ought to hope in him in their greatest straits; and, since he is their only Saviour, they ought to hope in him alone. They plead likewise, "<hi type="italic">Thou art in the midst of us;</hi> we have the special tokens of thy presence with us, thy temple, thy ark, thy oracles, and <hi type="italic">we are called by the name,</hi> the <hi type="italic">Israel</hi> of God; and therefore we have reason to hope thou wilt not leave us; <hi type="italic">we are thine, save us.</hi> Thy name is called upon us, and therefore what evils we are under reflect dishonour upon thee, as if thou wert not able to relieve thy own." The prophet had often told the people that their profession of religion would not protect them from the judgments of God; yet here he pleads it with God, as Moses, <reference osisRef="Exod.32.11">Exod. xxxii. 11</reference>. Even this may go far as to temporal punishments with a God of mercy. <hi type="italic">Valeat quantum valere potest—Let the plea avail as far as is proper.</hi> (2.) It therefore grieves them to think that he does not appear for their deliverance; and, though they do not charge it upon him as unrighteous, they humbly plead it with him why he should be gracious, for the glory of his own name. For otherwise he will seem, [1.] Unconcerned for his own people: <hi type="italic">What will the Egyptians say?</hi> they will say, "Israel's hope and Saviour does not mind them; he has become <hi type="italic">as a stranger in the land,</hi> that does not at all interest himself in its interests; his temple, which he called <hi type="italic">his rest for ever,</hi> is no more so, but he is in it <hi type="italic">as a wayfaring man, that turns aside to tarry but for a night</hi> in an inn, which he never enquires into the affairs of, nor is in any care about." Though God never is, yet he sometimes seems to be, as if he cared not what became of his church: Christ slept when his disciples were in storm. [2.] Incapable of giving them any relief. The enemies once said, Because the Lord <hi type="italic">was not able to bring</hi> his people to Canaan, he let them <hi type="italic">perish in the wilderness</hi> (<reference osisRef="Num.14.16">Num. xiv. 16</reference>); so now they will say, "Either his wisdom or his power fails him; either he is <hi type="italic">as a man astonished</hi> (who, though he has the reason of a man, yet, being astonished, is quite at a loss and at his wits' end) or as a <hi type="italic">mighty man</hi> who is overpowered by such as are more mighty, and therefore <hi type="italic">cannot save;</hi> though mighty, yet a man, and therefore having his power limited." Either of these would be a most insufferable reproach to the divine perfections; and therefore, why has the God that we are sure <hi type="italic">is in the midst of us</hi> become <hi type="italic">as a stranger?</hi> Why does the almighty God seem as if he were no more than a mighty man, who, when he is astonished, though he would, yet cannot save? It becomes us in prayer to show ourselves concerned more for God's glory than for our own comfort. Lord, <hi type="italic">what wilt thou do unto thy great name?</hi>
entries.b86dc648befbb99d18000899bc7c3ee643064f9d: <div eID="gen17504" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Divine Threatenings. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17505" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">10</hi> Thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto this people, Thus have they loved to wander, they have not refrained their feet, therefore the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> doth not accept them; he will now remember their iniquity, and visit their sins. <hi type="super">11</hi> Then said the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> unto me, Pray not for this people for <hi type="italic">their</hi> good. <hi type="super">12</hi> When they fast, I will not hear their cry; and when they offer burnt offering and an oblation, I will not accept them: but I will consume them by the sword, and by the famine, and by the pestilence. <hi type="super">13</hi> Then said I, Ah, Lord <hi type="small-caps">God</hi> ! behold, the prophets say unto them, Ye shall not see the sword, neither shall ye have famine; but I will give you assured peace in this place. <hi type="super">14</hi> Then the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> said unto me, The prophets prophesy lies in my name: I sent them not, neither have I commanded them, neither spake unto them: they prophesy unto you a false vision and divination, and a thing of nought, and the deceit of their heart. <hi type="super">15</hi> Therefore thus saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> concerning the prophets that prophesy in my name, and I sent them not, yet they say, Sword and famine shall not be in this land; By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the people to whom they prophesy shall be cast out in the streets of Jerusalem because of the famine and the sword; and they shall have none to bury them, them, their wives, nor their sons, nor their daughters: for I will pour their wickedness upon them. <div eID="gen17505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17506" type="x-p"/> The dispute between God and his prophet, in this chapter, seems to be like that between the owner and the dresser of the vineyard concerning the barren fig-tree, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.7">Luke xiii. 7</reference>. The justice of the owner condemns it to be cut down; the clemency of the dresser intercedes for a reprieve. Jeremiah had been earnest with God, in prayer, to return in mercy to this people. Now here, <div eID="gen17506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17507" type="x-p"/> I. God overrules the plea which he had offered in their favour, and shows him that it would not hold. In answer to it thus he says concerning <hi type="italic">this people,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.10">v. 10</reference>. He does not say, concerning <hi type="italic">my people,</hi> for he disowns them, because they had broken covenant with him. It is true they were <hi type="italic">called by his name,</hi> and had the tokens of his presence among them; but they had sinned, and provoked God to withdraw. This the prophet had owned, and had hoped to obtain mercy for them, notwithstanding this, through intercession and sacrifice; therefore God here tells him, 1. That they were not duly qualified for a pardon. The prophet had owned that <hi type="italic">their backslidings were many;</hi> and, though they were so, yet there was hope for them if they returned. But <hi type="italic">this people</hi> show no disposition at all to return; they have wandered, and <hi type="italic">they have loved to wander;</hi> their backslidings have been their choice and their pleasure, which should have been their shame and pain, and therefore they will be their ruin. They cannot expect God should take up his rest with them when they take such delight in going astray from him after their idols. It is not through necessity or inadvertency that they wander, but they love to wander. Sinners are wanderers from God; their wanderings forfeit God's favour, but it is their loving to wander that quite cuts them off from it. They were told what their wanderings would come to that one sin would hurry them on to another, and all to ruin; and yet they have not taken warning and <hi type="italic">refrained their feet.</hi> So far were they from returning to their God that neither his prophets nor his judgments could prevail upon them to give themselves the least check in a sinful pursuit. This is that for which God is now reckoning with them. When he denies them rain from heaven he is <hi type="italic">remembering their iniquity</hi> and <hi type="italic">visiting their sin;</hi> that is it for which their <hi type="italic">fruitful land</hi> is thus <hi type="italic">turned into barrenness.</hi> 2. That they had no reason to expect that the God they had rejected should accept them; no, not though they betook themselves to fasting and prayer and put themselves to the expense of burnt-offerings and sacrifice: <hi type="italic">The Lord doth not accept them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.10">v. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">He takes no pleasure in them</hi> (so the word is); for what pleasure can the holy God take in those that take pleasure in his rivals, in any service, in any society, rather than his? "<hi type="italic">When they fast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">v. 12</reference>), which is a proper expression of repentance and reformation,—<hi type="italic">when they offer a burnt offering and an oblation,</hi> which was designed to be an expression of faith in a Mediator,—though their prayers be thus enforced, and offered up in those vehicles that used to be acceptable, yet, because they do not proceed from humble, penitent, and renewed hearts, but still they <hi type="italic">love to wander,</hi> therefore <hi type="italic">I will not hear their cry,</hi> be it ever so loud; <hi type="italic">nor will I accept them,</hi> neither their persons nor their performances." It had been long since declared, <hi type="italic">The sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord;</hi> and those only are <hi type="italic">accepted</hi> that <hi type="italic">do well,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.4.7">Gen. iv. 7</reference>. 3. That they had forfeited all benefit by the prophet's prayers for them because they had not regarded his preaching to them. This is the meaning of that repeated prohibition given to the prophet (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">Pray not thou for this people for their good,</hi> as before, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.15">ch. vii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.11.14">xi. 14</reference>. This did not forbid him thus to express his <hi type="italic">good-will</hi> to them (Moses continued to intercede for Israel after God had said, <hi type="italic">Let me alone,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Exod. xxxii. 10</reference>), but it forbade them to expect any good effect from it as long as they <hi type="italic">turned away their ear from hearing the law.</hi> Thus was the doom of the impenitent ratified, as that of Saul's rejection was by that word to Samuel, <hi type="italic">When wilt thou cease to mourn for Saul?</hi> It therefore follows (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">v. 12</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will consume them,</hi> not only by this famine, but by the further sore judgments of sword and pestilence; for God has many arrows in his quiver, and those that will not be convinced and reclaimed by one shall be consumed by another. <div eID="gen17507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17508" type="x-p"/> II. The prophet offers another plea in excuse for the people's obstinacy, and it is but an excuse, but he was willing to say whatever their case would bear; it is this, That the prophets, who pretended a commission from heaven, imposed upon them, and flattered them with assurances of peace though they went on in their sinful way, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13">v. 13</reference>. He speaks of it with lamentation: "<hi type="italic">Ah! Lord God,</hi> the poor people seem willing to take notice of what comes in thy name, and there are those who in thy name tell them that they <hi type="italic">shall not see the sword nor famine;</hi> and they say it as from thee, with all the gravity and confidence of prophets: <hi type="italic">I will</hi> continue you <hi type="italic">in this place,</hi> and will <hi type="italic">give you assured peace</hi> here, peace of truth. I tell them the contrary; but I am one against many, and every one is apt to credit that which makes for them; therefore, Lord, pity and spare them, for <hi type="italic">their leaders cause them to err.</hi>" This excuse would have been of some weight if they had not had warning given them, before, of false prophets, and rules by which to distinguish them; so that if they were deceived it was entirely their own fault. But this teaches us, as far as we can with truth, to make the best of bad, and judge as charitably of others as their case will bear. <div eID="gen17508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17509" type="x-p"/> III. God not only overrules this plea, but condemns both the blind leaders and the blind followers to fall together into the ditch. 1. God disowns the flatteries (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.14">v. 14</reference>): <hi type="italic">They prophesy lies in my name.</hi> They had no commission from God to prophesy at all: <hi type="italic">I neither sent them, nor commanded them, nor spoke unto them.</hi> They never were employed to go on any errand at all from God; he never made himself known to them, much less by them to the people; never any word of the Lord came to them, no call, no warrant, no instruction, much less did he send them on this errand, to rock them asleep in security. No; men may flatter themselves, and Satan may flatter them, but God never does. It is <hi type="italic">a false vision, and a thing of nought.</hi> Note, What is false and groundless is vain and worthless. The vision that is not true, be it ever so pleasing, is good for nothing; it is the <hi type="italic">deceit of their heart,</hi> a spider's web spun out of their own bowels, and in it they think to shelter themselves, but it will be swept away in a moment and prove a great cheat. Those that oppose their own thoughts of God's word (God indeed says so, but they think otherwise) walk in the <hi type="italic">deceit of their heart,</hi> and it will be their ruin. 2. He passes sentence upon the flatterers, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.15">v. 15</reference>. As for the prophets, who put this abuse upon the people by telling them they shall have peace, and this affront upon God by telling them so in God's name, let them know that they shall have no peace themselves. They shall fall first by those very judgments which they have flattered others with the hopes of an exemption from. They undertook to warrant people that <hi type="italic">sword and famine</hi> should <hi type="italic">not be in the land;</hi> but it shall soon appear how little their warrants are good for, when they themselves shall be cut off by sword and famine. How should they secure others or foretel peace to them when they cannot secure themselves, nor have such a foresight of their own calamities as to get out of the way of them? Note, The sorest punishment await those who promise sinners impunity in their sinful ways. 3. He lays the flattered under the same doom: The <hi type="italic">people to whom they prophesy lies,</hi> and who willingly suffer themselves to be thus imposed upon, <hi type="italic">shall die by sword and famine,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.16">v. 16</reference>. Note, The unbelief of the deceived, with all the falsehood of the deceivers, shall not make the divine threatenings of no effect; sword and famine will come, whatever they say to the contrary; and those will be least safe that are most secure. Impenitent sinners will not escape the damnation of hell by saying that they can never believe there is such a thing, but will feel what they will not fear. It is threatened that this people shall not only fall by <hi type="italic">sword and famine,</hi> but that they shall be as it were hanged up in chains, as monuments of that divine justice which they set at defiance; their bodies shall be <hi type="italic">cast out,</hi> even <hi type="italic">in the streets of Jerusalem,</hi> which of all places, one would think, should be kept clear from such nuisances: there they shall lie unburied; their nearest relations, who should do them that last office of love, being so poor that they cannot afford it, or so weakened with hunger that they are not able to attend it, or so overwhelmed with grief that they have no heart to it, or so destitute of natural affection that they will not pay them so much respect. Thus will God <hi type="italic">pour their wickedness upon them,</hi> that is, the punishment of their wickedness; the full vials of God's wrath shall be poured upon them, to which they have made themselves obnoxious. Note, When sinners are overwhelmed with trouble they must in it see their own wickedness poured upon them. This refers to the wickedness both of the false prophets and of the people; the blind lead the blind, and both fall together into the ditch, where they will be miserable comforters one to another.
entries.8ffa410f15b010b5d2823f07a906dbfcda38bbdd: <div eID="gen17509" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Prophet's Intercession. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 606.)</title> <div sID="gen17510" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">17</hi> Therefore thou shalt say this word unto them; Let mine eyes run down with tears night and day, and let them not cease: for the virgin daughter of my people is broken with a great breach, with a very grievous blow. <hi type="super">18</hi> If I go forth into the field, then behold the slain with the sword! and if I enter into the city, then behold them that are sick with famine! yea, both the prophet and the priest go about into a land that they know not. <hi type="super">19</hi> Hast thou utterly rejected Judah? hath thy soul loathed Zion? why hast thou smitten us, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no healing for us? we looked for peace, and <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no good; and for the time of healing, and behold trouble! <hi type="super">20</hi> We acknowledge, <hi type="small-caps">O Lord</hi> , our wickedness, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the iniquity of our fathers: for we have sinned against thee. <hi type="super">21</hi> Do not abhor <hi type="italic">us,</hi> for thy name's sake, do not disgrace the throne of thy glory: remember, break not thy covenant with us. <hi type="super">22</hi> Are there <hi type="italic">any</hi> among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain? or can the heavens give showers? <hi type="italic">art</hi> not thou he, O <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God? therefore we will wait upon thee: for thou hast made all these <hi type="italic">things.</hi> <div eID="gen17510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17511" type="x-p"/> The present deplorable state of Judah and Jerusalem is here made the matter of the prophet's lamentation (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.17-Jer.14.18">v. 17, 18</reference>) and the occasion of his prayer and intercession for them (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">v. 19</reference>), and I am willing to hope that the latter, as well as the former, was by divine direction, and that these words (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.17">v. 17</reference>), <hi type="italic">Thus shalt thou say unto them</hi> (or <hi type="italic">concerning them,</hi> or <hi type="italic">in their hearing</hi>), refer to the intercession, as well as to the lamentation, and then it amounts to a revocation of the directions given to the prophet not to pray for them, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.11">v. 11</reference>. However, it is plain, by the prayers we find in these verses, that the prophet did not understand it as a prohibition, but only as a discouragement, like that <reference osisRef="1John.5.16">1 John v. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">I do not say he shall pray for that.</hi> Here, <div eID="gen17511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17512" type="x-p"/> I. The prophet stands weeping over the ruins of his country; God directs him to do so, that, showing himself affected, he might, if possible, affect them with the foresight of the calamities that were coming upon them. Jeremiah must say it not only to himself, but to them too: <hi type="italic">Let my eyes run down with tears,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.17">v. 17</reference>. Thus he must signify to them that he certainly foresaw <hi type="italic">the sword</hi> coming, and another sort of famine, more grievous even than this which they were now groaning under; this was in the country for want of rain, that would be in the city through the straitness of the siege. The prophet speaks as if he already saw the miseries attending the descent which the Chaldeans made upon them: <hi type="italic">The virgin daughter of my people,</hi> that is as dear to me as a daughter to her father, <hi type="italic">is broken with a great breach, with a very grievous blow,</hi> much greater and more grievous than any she has yet sustained; for (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.18">v. 18</reference>) <hi type="italic">in the field</hi> multitudes lie dead that were <hi type="italic">slain by the sword,</hi> and in the city multitudes lie dying for want of food. Doleful spectacles! "<hi type="italic">The prophets and the priests,</hi> the false prophets that flattered them with their lies and the wicked priests that persecuted the true prophets, are now expelled their country, and <hi type="italic">go about</hi> either as prisoners and captives, whithersoever their conquerors lead them, or as fugitives and vagabonds, wherever they can find shelter and relief, <hi type="italic">in a land that they know not.</hi>" Some understand this of the true prophets, Ezekiel and Daniel, that were carried to Babylon with the rest. The prophet's eyes must run down <hi type="italic">with tears day and night,</hi> in prospect of this, that the people might be convinced, not only that this woeful day would infallibly come, and would be a very woeful day indeed, but that he was far from desiring it, and would as gladly have brought them messages of peace as their false prophets, if he might have had warrant from heaven to do it. Note, Because God, though he inflicts death on sinners, yet delights not in it, it becomes his ministers, though in his name they pronounce the death of sinners, yet sadly to lament it. <div eID="gen17512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17513" type="x-p"/> II. He stands up to make intercession for them; for who knows but God will yet return and repent? While there is life there is hope, and room for prayer. And, though there were many among them who neither prayed themselves nor valued the prophet's prayers, yet there were some who were better affected, would join with him in his devotions, and set the seal of their <hi type="italic">Amen</hi> to them. <div eID="gen17513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17514" type="x-p"/> 1. He humbly expostulates with God concerning the present deplorableness of their case, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">v. 19</reference>. It was very sad, for, (1.) Their expectations from their God failed them; they thought he had avouched Judah to be his, but now, it seems, he has <hi type="italic">utterly rejected</hi> it, and cast it off, will not own any relation to it nor concern for it. They thought Zion was the beloved of his soul, was his rest for ever; but now <hi type="italic">his soul</hi> even <hi type="italic">loathes Zion,</hi> loathes even the services there performed, for the sake of the sins there committed. (2.) Then no marvel that all their other expectations failed them: <hi type="italic">They were smitten,</hi> and their wounds were multiplied, but there was <hi type="italic">no healing</hi> for them; they <hi type="italic">looked for peace,</hi> because after a storm there usually comes a calm and fair weather, after a long fit of wet; but <hi type="italic">there was no good,</hi> things went still worse and worse. They looked for a <hi type="italic">healing time,</hi> but could not gain so much as a <hi type="italic">breathing time. "Behold, trouble</hi> at the door, by which we hoped peace would enter. And is it so then? <hi type="italic">Hast thou</hi> indeed <hi type="italic">rejected Judah?</hi> Justly thou mightest. <hi type="italic">Hath thy soul loathed Zion?</hi> We deserve it should. But wilt thou not at length in wrath remember mercy?" <div eID="gen17514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17515" type="x-p"/> 2. He makes a penitent confession of sin, speaking that language which they all should have spoken, though but few did (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">We acknowledge our wickedness,</hi> the abounding wickedness of our land <hi type="italic">and the iniquity of our fathers,</hi> which we have imitated, and therefore justly smart for. <hi type="italic">We know, we acknowledge,</hi> that <hi type="italic">we have sinned against thee,</hi> and therefore thou art just in all that is brought upon us; but, because we confess our sins, we hope to find thee faithful and just in forgiving our sins." <div eID="gen17515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17516" type="x-p"/> 3. He deprecates God's displeasure, and by faith appeals to his honour and promise, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.21">v. 21</reference>. His petition is, "<hi type="italic">Do not abhor us;</hi> though thou afflict us, <hi type="italic">do not abhor us;</hi> though thy hand by turned <hi type="italic">against</hi> us, let not thy heart be so, nor let thy mind be alienated from us." They own God might justly abhor them, they had rendered themselves odious in his eyes; yet, when they pray, <hi type="italic">Do not abhor us,</hi> they mean, "Receive us into favour again. <hi type="italic">Let not thy soul loathe Zion,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">v. 19</reference>. Let not our incense be an abomination." They appeal, (1.) To the honour of God, the honour of his scriptures, by which he has made himself known—his <hi type="italic">word,</hi> which he has <hi type="italic">magnified above all his name: "Do not abhor us, for thy name's sake,</hi> that the name of thine by which we are called and which we call upon." The honour of his sanctuary is pleaded: "Lord, do not abhor us, for that will <hi type="italic">disgrace the throne of thy glory</hi>" (the temple, which is called <hi type="italic">a glorious high throne from the beginning,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.17.12">ch. xvii. 12</reference>); let not that which has been the <hi type="italic">joy of the whole earth</hi> be made a <hi type="italic">hissing</hi> and an <hi type="italic">astonishment.</hi> We deserve to have disgrace put upon us, but let it not be so as to reflect upon thyself; let not the desolations of the temple give occasion to the heathen to reproach him that used to be worshipped there, as if he could not, or would not, protect it, or as if the gods of the Chaldeans had been too hard for him. Note, Good men lay the credit of religion, and its profession in the world, nearer their hearts than any private interest or concern of their own; and those are powerful pleas in prayer which are fetched thence and great supports to faith. We may be sure that God will not <hi type="italic">disgrace the throne of his glory</hi> on earth; nor will he eclipse the glory of his throne by one providence without soon making it shine forth, and more brightly than before, by another. God will be no loser in his honour at the long-run. (2.) To the promise of God; of this they are humbly bold to put him in mind: <hi type="italic">Remember thy covenant with us, and break not</hi> that covenant. Not that they had any distrust of his fidelity, or that they thought he needed to be put in mind of his promise to them, but what he had said he would plead with himself they take the liberty to plead with him. <hi type="italic">Then will I remember my covenant,</hi> <reference osisRef="Lev.26.42">Lev. xxvi. 42</reference>. <div eID="gen17516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17517" type="x-p"/> 4. He professes a dependence upon God for the mercy of rain, which they were now in want of, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.22">v. 22</reference>. If they have forfeited their interest in him as their God in covenant, yet they will not let go their hold on him as the God of nature. (1.) They will never make application to the idols of the heathen, for that would be foolish and fruitless: <hi type="italic">Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles that can cause rain?</hi> No; in a time of great drought in Israel, Baal, though all Israel presented their prayers to him in the days of Ahab, could not relieve them; it was that God only who <hi type="italic">answered by fire</hi> that could answer <hi type="italic">by water</hi> too. (2.) They will not terminate their regards in second causes, nor expect supply from nature only: <hi type="italic">Can the heavens give showers?</hi> No, not without orders from the God of heaven; for it is he that has the key of the clouds, that <hi type="italic">opens the bottles of heaven</hi> and <hi type="italic">waters the earth from his chambers.</hi> But, (3.) All their expectation therefore is from him and their confidence in him: "<hi type="italic">Art not thou he, O Lord our God!</hi> from whom we may expect succour and to whom we must apply? Art thou not he that <hi type="italic">causest rain</hi> and <hi type="italic">givest showers?</hi> For <hi type="italic">thou hast made all these things;</hi> thou gavest them being, and therefore thou givest them law and hast them all at thy command; thou madest that moisture in nature which is in a constant circulation to serve the intentions of Providence, and thou directest it, and makest what use thou pleasest of it; <hi type="italic">therefore we will wait upon thee,</hi> and upon thee only; we will <hi type="italic">ask of the Lord rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zech. x. 1</reference>. We will trust in him to give it to us in due time, and be willing to tarry his time; it is fit that we should, and it will not be in vain to do so." Note, The sovereignty of God should engage, and his all-sufficiency encourage, our attendance on him and our expectations from him at all times.  <chapter eID="Jer.14"/> <div eID="gen17517" type="x-p"/>

entries.949395d17b576fa0b33d5a4c9e4f61bff94b57d6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9904"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 14</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Jer.14.1-Jer.14.22">Jr 14:1-22</reference>. Prophecies on the Occasion of a Drought Sent in Judgment on Judea.</title> <div sID="gen17587" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9904"/>1. Literally, "That which was the word of Jehovah to Jeremiah concerning the dearth"<div eID="gen17587" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17588" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">drought--</hi>literally, the "withholdings," namely, of rain (<reference osisRef="Deut.11.17">De 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.7.13">2Ch 7:13</reference>). This word should be used especially of the withholding of rain because rain is in those regions of all things the one chiefly needed (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jr 17:8</reference>, Margin). <div eID="gen17588" type="x-p"/>
entries.a85255de2e860c23649b9e3048bc0b931ca4da5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9905"/><div sID="gen17589" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9905"/><hi type="bold">2. gates--</hi>The place of public concourse in each city looks sad, as being no longer frequented (<reference osisRef="Isa.3.26">Is 3:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.4">24:4</reference>).<div eID="gen17589" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17590" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">black--</hi>that is, they mourn (blackness being indicative of sorrow), (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.21">Jr 8:21</reference>).<div eID="gen17590" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17591" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">unto the ground--</hi>bowing towards it.<div eID="gen17591" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17592" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cry--</hi>of distress (<reference osisRef="1Sam.5.12">1Sa 5:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.24.11">Is 24:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17592" type="x-p"/>
entries.3f7f68efb13fb2f35e0b1e1a898e2cff47cf679d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9906"/><div sID="gen17593" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9906"/><hi type="bold">3. little ones--</hi>rather, "their inferiors," that is, domestics.<div eID="gen17593" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17594" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pits--</hi>cisterns for collecting rain water, often met with in the East where there are no springs.<div eID="gen17594" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17595" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covered ... heads--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>). A sign of humiliation and mourning. <div eID="gen17595" type="x-p"/>
entries.50059bacce38eaf42a1c5c02f3498a44f7de9998: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9907"/><div sID="gen17596" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9907"/>5. The brute creation is reduced to the utmost extremity for the want of food. The "hind," famed for her affection to her young, abandons them. <div eID="gen17596" type="x-p"/>
entries.dfff6cef4526b2355977f8bb7e3a7f472260b383: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9908"/><div sID="gen17597" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9908"/><hi type="bold">6. wild asses--</hi>They repair to "the high places" most exposed to the winds, which they "snuff in" to relieve their thirst.<div eID="gen17597" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17598" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">dragons--</hi>jackals [Henderson].<div eID="gen17598" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17599" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">eyes--</hi>which are usually most keen in detecting grass or water from the "heights," so much so that the traveller guesses from their presence that there must be herbage and water near; but now "their eyes fail." Rather the reference is to the great boas and python serpents which raise a large portion of their body up in a vertical column ten or twelve feet high, to survey the neighborhood above the surrounding bushes, while with open jaws they drink in the air. These giant serpents originated the widely spread notions which typified the deluge and all destructive agents under the form of a dragon or monster serpent; hence, the dragon temples always near water, in Asia, Africa, and Britain; for example, at Abury, in Wiltshire; a symbol of the ark is often associated with the dragon as the preserver from the waters [Kitto, Biblical Cyclopædia]. <div eID="gen17599" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff4f1870e7100013c7e3efacadf08fb2d33c0469: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9909"/><div sID="gen17600" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9909"/><hi type="bold">7. do thou it--</hi>what we beg of Thee; interpose to remove the drought. Jeremiah pleads in the name of his nation (<reference osisRef="Ps.109.21">Psa 109:21</reference>). So "work for us," absolutely used (<reference osisRef="1Sam.14.6">1Sa 14:6</reference>).<div eID="gen17600" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17601" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">for thy name's sake--</hi>"for our backslidings are so many" that we cannot urge Thee for the sake of our doings, but for the glory of Thy name; lest, if Thou give us not aid, it should be said it was owing to Thy want of power (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.9">Jos 7:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.79.9">Psa 79:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.106.8">106:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.9">Is 48:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.20.44">Eze 20:44</reference>). The same appeal to God's mercy, "for His name's sake," as our only hope, since our sin precludes trust in ourselves, occurs in <reference osisRef="Ps.25.11">Psa 25:11</reference>. <div eID="gen17601" type="x-p"/>
entries.cd91a9bcae31887c21a857f92beb17130402d437: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9910"/><div sID="gen17602" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9910"/>8. The reference is, not to the faith of Israel which had almost ceased, but to the promise and everlasting covenant of God. None but the true Israel make God their "hope." (<reference osisRef="Jer.17.13">Jr 17:13</reference>).<div eID="gen17602" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17603" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">turneth aside to tarry--</hi>The traveller cares little for the land he tarries but a night in; but Thou hast promised to dwell always in the midst of Thy people (<reference osisRef="2Chr.33.7">2Ch 33:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.33.8">8</reference>). Maurer translates, "spreadeth," namely, his tent. <div eID="gen17603" type="x-p"/>
entries.43dcb4bbdc6c05a5ae5aa78ad1d1e430cdf13f0c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9911"/><div sID="gen17604" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9911"/><hi type="bold">9. astonied--</hi>like a "mighty man," at other times able to help (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.1">Is 59:1</reference>), but now stunned by a sudden calamity so as to disappoint the hopes drawn from him.<div eID="gen17604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">art in the midst of us--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Exod.29.45">Ex 29:45</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.29.46">46</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lev.26.11">Le 26:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.26.12">12</reference>).<div eID="gen17605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17606" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">called by thy name--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.9.18">Da 9:18</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.9.19">19</reference>) as Thine own peculiar people (<reference osisRef="Deut.9.29">De 9:29</reference>). <div eID="gen17606" type="x-p"/>
entries.eb1471cb2d0339227ca52b272f588742df6bd954: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9912"/><div sID="gen17607" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9912"/>10. Jehovah's reply to the prayer (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.7-Jer.14.9">Jr 14:7-9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.2.23-Jer.2.25">Jr 2:23-25</reference>).<div eID="gen17607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17608" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thus--</hi>So greatly.<div eID="gen17608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17609" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">loved--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>).<div eID="gen17609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17610" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">not refrained ... feet--</hi>They did not obey God's command; "withhold thy foot" (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.25">Jr 2:25</reference>), namely, from following after idols.<div eID="gen17610" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17611" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">remember ... iniquity--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Hos.8.13">Ho 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">9:9</reference>). Their sin is so great, God must punish them. <div eID="gen17611" type="x-p"/>
entries.2aa402e21b5787d42281bf1372af3c6375f63f7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9913"/><div sID="gen17612" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9913"/>11. (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.16">Jr 7:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.10">Ex 32:10</reference>). <div eID="gen17612" type="x-p"/>
entries.8bdcba442f7c8390466817108a59db90d8c7d0a9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9914"/><div sID="gen17613" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9914"/><hi type="bold">12. not hear--</hi>because their prayers are hypocritical: their hearts are still idolatrous. God never refuses to hear real prayer (<reference osisRef="Jer.7.21">Jr 7:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.7.22">22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.1.28">Pr 1:28</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.1.15">Is 1:15</reference>; 58:3).<div eID="gen17613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17614" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sword ... famine ... pestilence--</hi>the three sorest judgments at once; any one of which would be enough for their ruin (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.12">2Sa 24:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Sam.24.13">13</reference>). <div eID="gen17614" type="x-p"/>
entries.6846e87fea518f47fa0e2c6ba9041520b35288b7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9915"/><div sID="gen17615" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9915"/>13. Jeremiah urges that much of the guilt of the people is due to the false prophets' influence.<div eID="gen17615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17616" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">assured peace--</hi>solid and lasting peace. Literally, "peace of truth" (<reference osisRef="Isa.39.8">Is 39:8</reference>). <div eID="gen17616" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Jer.5.12">Jr 5:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.5.13">13</reference>).<div eID="gen17618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17619" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">By sword and famine ... consumed--</hi>retribution in kind both to the false prophets and to their hearers (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.16">Jr 14:16</reference>). <div eID="gen17619" type="x-p"/>
entries.f164e572d39e96d2b604ad38ea588606f7b2b9cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9918"/><div sID="gen17620" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9918"/><hi type="bold">16. none to bury--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.79.3">Psa 79:3</reference>).<div eID="gen17620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17621" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">pour their wickedness--</hi>that is, the punishment incurred by their wickedness (<reference osisRef="Jer.2.19">Jr 2:19</reference>). <div eID="gen17621" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd1ebcf889c6057ba18605e731423b3e99b49f5c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9919"/><div sID="gen17622" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9919"/>17. (<reference osisRef="Jer.9.1">Jr 9:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.1.16">La 1:16</reference>). Jeremiah is desired to weep ceaselessly for the calamities coming on his nation (called a "virgin," as being heretofore never under foreign yoke), (<reference osisRef="Isa.23.4">Is 23:4</reference>). <div eID="gen17622" type="x-p"/>
entries.e7cf45427e3e6635bfc4ca862e486870fff7f2e2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9920"/><div sID="gen17623" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9920"/><hi type="bold">18. go about--</hi>that is, shall have to migrate into a land of exile. Horsley translates, "go trafficking about the land (see <reference osisRef="Jer.5.31">Jr 5:31</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.2">2Co 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.3">2Pe 2:3</reference>), and take no knowledge" (that is, pay no regard to the miseries before their eyes) (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.3">Is 1:3</reference>; 58:3). If the literal sense of the Hebrew verb be retained, I would with English Version understand the words as referring to the exile to Babylon; thus, "the prophet and the priest shall have to go to a strange land to practise their religious traffic (<reference osisRef="Isa.56.11">Is 56:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.2">Eze 34:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.3">3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mic.3.11">Mi 3:11</reference>). <div eID="gen17623" type="x-p"/>

The people plead with God, Jeremiah being forbidden to do so.<div eID="gen17624" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17625" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">no healing--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.15.18">Jr 15:18</reference>).<div eID="gen17625" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17626" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">peace ... no good--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Jer.8.15">Jr 8:15</reference>). <div eID="gen17626" type="x-p"/>

entries.758d1d25a505eb3b66c156e788385ea33ad37f66: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9923"/><div sID="gen17628" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9923"/><hi type="bold">21. us--</hi>"the throne of Thy glory" may be the object of "abhor not" ("reject not"); or "Zion" (<reference osisRef="Jer.14.19">Jr 14:19</reference>).<div eID="gen17628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17629" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">throne of thy glory--</hi>Jerusalem, or, the temple, called God's "footstool" and "habitation" (<reference osisRef="1Chr.28.2">1Ch 28:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.132.5">Psa 132:5</reference>).<div eID="gen17629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17630" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">thy covenant--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.106.45">Psa 106:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.19">Da 9:19</reference>). <div eID="gen17630" type="x-p"/>
entries.bc15a84338751c483b7a3eeadb2f350972d5a1f6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv9924"/><div sID="gen17631" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv9924"/><hi type="bold">22. vanities--</hi>idols (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.21">De 32:21</reference>).<div eID="gen17631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17632" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rain--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Zech.10.1">Zec 10:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.10.2">2</reference>).<div eID="gen17632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17633" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heavens--</hi>namely, of themselves without God (<reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Mt 5:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Ac 14:17</reference>); they are not the First Cause, and ought not to be deified, as they were by the heathen. The disjunctive "or" favors Calvin's explanation: "Not even the heavens themselves can give rain, much less can the idol vanities."<div eID="gen17633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17634" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">art not thou he--</hi>namely, who canst give rain? <chapter eID="Jer.14"/>

entries.685ce1a36e2111d00fedb60adab1cd054aa24422: <div eID="gen29624" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen29625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29626" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen29625" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen29627" type="x-p"/> This chapter begins with foretelling a drought that should greatly distress the land of Judea, the effects of which are described in a most pathetic manner, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1-Jer.14.6">Jer 14:1-6</reference>. The prophet then, in the people's name, makes a confession of sins, and supplication for pardon, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.7-Jer.14.9">Jer 14:7-9</reference>. But God declares his purpose to punish, forbidding Jeremiah to pray for the people, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.10-Jer.14.12">Jer 14:10-12</reference>. False prophets are then complained of, and threatened with destruction, as are also those who attend to them, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.13-Jer.14.16">Jer 14:13-16</reference>. The prophet, therefore, bewails their misery, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.17">Jer 14:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.18">Jer 14:18</reference>; and though he had just now been forbidden to intercede for them, yet, like a tender pastor, who could not cease to be concerned for their welfare, he falls on the happy expedient of introducing themselves as supplicating in their own name that mercy which he was not allowed to ask in his, <reference osisRef="Jer.14.19-Jer.14.22">Jer 14:19-22</reference>. <div eID="gen29627" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29628" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen29628" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29629" type="x-p"/> The word - that came - concerning the dearth - This discourse is supposed to have been delivered, after the fourth year of Jehoiakim. Concerning the dearth. We have no historic record of any dearth that may fall in with the time of this prophecy, and perhaps it does not refer to any particular dearth: but this was a calamity to which Judea was very liable. They had ordinarily very dry summers, for scarcely any rain fell from April to the middle of October; and during much of this time, the rivers were generally either very low or entirely dry. They kept the rain of the winter in tanks and reservoirs; and if little fell in winter, a dearth was unavoidable. See an account of a dearth in the time of Elijah, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.5">1Kgs 18:5</reference>, through which almost all the cattle were lost.
entries.fba16a0b9112d60397705f380f71c7ff6699e80f: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen29629" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29630" type="x-p"/> The gates thereof languish - The gates being the places of public resort, they are put here for the people. <div eID="gen29630" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29631" type="x-p"/> They are black unto the ground - Covered from head to foot with a black garment, the emblem of sorrow and calamity.
entries.a707e15f4d10dfe727e8cd1b7c1573bb7bb0aab4: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen29631" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29632" type="x-p"/> Their nobles have sent their little ones - So general was this calamity, that the servants no longer attended to their lords, but every one was interested alone for himself; and the nobles of the land were obliged to employ their own children to scour the land, to see if any water could be found in the tanks or the pits. In the dearth in the time of Elijah, Ahab the king, and Obadiah his counselor, were obliged to traverse the land themselves, in order to find out water to keep their cattle alive. This and the three following verses give a lively but distressing picture of this dearth and its effects.
entries.b63f2923002e810ec2a5f6b49407f0dedd9bef89: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen29632" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29633" type="x-p"/> The ground is chapt - The cracks in the earth before the descent of the rains are in some places a cubit wide, and deep enough to receive the greater part of a human body.
entries.cb7869a5cac2816a297a11710309bc34cd8cec2b: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen29633" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29634" type="x-p"/> Snuffed up the wind like dragons - תנים tannim here probably means the hippopotamus, who, after feeding under the water, is obliged to come to the surface in order to take in fresh draughts of air; or it may mean the wild asses.
entries.2446e46092b82a5b4f30dfd31193c2573fd1ddcc: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen29634" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29635" type="x-p"/> O Lord, though our iniquities testify against us - We deeply acknowledge that we have sinned, and deserve nothing but death. Yet act for thy name's sake - work in our behalf, that we perish not.
entries.94d2a256d669745ae9582d28795c726a9e28e984: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen29635" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29636" type="x-p"/> O the hope of Israel - O thou who art the only object of the hope of this people. <div eID="gen29636" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29637" type="x-p"/> The Savior thereof in time of trouble - Who hast never yet abandoned them that seek thee. <div eID="gen29637" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29638" type="x-p"/> Why shouldest thou be as a stranger in the land - As one who has no interest in the prosperity and safety of the country. <div eID="gen29638" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29639" type="x-p"/> And as a way-faring man - A traveler on his journey. <div eID="gen29639" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29640" type="x-p"/> That turneth aside to tarry for a night? - Who stays the shortest time he can; and takes up his lodging in a tent or caravanserai, for the dead of the night, that he may pursue his journey by break of day. Instead of dwelling among us, thou hast scarcely paid the most transient visit to thy land. O come once more, and dwell among us.
entries.2e1087a623bfb9494586c65be7334db1e04483a4: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen29640" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29641" type="x-p"/> Yet thou, O Lord, art in the midst of us - Thy ark, temple, and sacred rites, are all here; and thou thyself, who art every where present, art here also: but alas! thou dost not reveal thyself as the Father of mercies, who forgivest iniquity, transgression, and sin. <div eID="gen29641" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29642" type="x-p"/> We are called by thy name; leave us not - Let us call thee our Father, and say thou to us, "Ye are my sons and daughters!" O leave us not!
entries.cb5c7f607706181a99789ef76af58f4a6e7f9faa: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen29642" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29643" type="x-p"/> Thus have they loved to wander - And the measure of your iniquity being now full, ye must be punished.
entries.92ccfa4b8556e9d2624bee00498bbf86607ce217: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen29643" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29644" type="x-p"/> Pray not for this people - They are ripe for destruction, intercede not for them. O, how dreadful is the state of that people in reference to whom the Lord says to his ministers, Pray not for them; or, what amounts nearly to a prohibition, withholds from his ministers the spirit of prayer and intercession in behalf of the people!
entries.b44814c0d3fc8a5ac1ec65b040bb1d3d6a31ddbc: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen29644" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29645" type="x-p"/> Ah, Lord God! behold, the prophets say unto them - True, Lord, they are exceedingly wicked; but the false prophets have deceived them; this is some mitigation of their offense. This plea God does not admit; and why? the people believed them, without having any proof of their Divine mission.
entries.dfa0d2afb46868383a9360a97f86f5014be89a8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen29645" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29646" type="x-p"/> The prophets prophesy lies - They say they have visions, but they have them by divination, and they are false. The people should know their character, and avoid them but they love to have it so, and will not be undeceived.
entries.294eef7b6fe9143a74cbfdfe1fb1b848c86e8070: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen29646" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29647" type="x-p"/> By sword and famine shall those prophets be consumed - Jeremiah had told Jehoiakim that, if he rebelled against Nebuchadnezzar, he should be overthrown, and the land wasted by sword and famine: the false prophets said there shall be neither sword nor famine, but peace and prosperity. The king believed them, and withheld the tribute. <div eID="gen29647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29648" type="x-p"/> Nebuchadnezzar, being incensed, invaded and destroyed the land; and the false prophets fell in these calamities. See <reference osisRef="2Kgs.25.3">2Kgs 25:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Lam.2.11-Lam.2.19">Lam 2:11-19</reference>.
entries.816e9f8039a94f86dc1280c52877b8d783e5510f: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen29648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29649" type="x-p"/> And the people - shall be cast out - They shall be destroyed, because they preferred their lying words to my truth, proclaimed by thee.
entries.590326471c90cf598fafbba1209ba7c6ddffb764: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen29649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29650" type="x-p"/> For the virgin daughter of my people is broken - First, the land was sadly distressed by Pharaoh-necho, king of Egypt. Secondly, it was laid under a heavy tribute by Nebuchadnezzar. And, thirdly, it was nearly desolated by a famine afterwards. In a few years all these calamities fell upon them; these might be well called a great breach, a very grievous blow.
entries.726dd47f73de655c1fbab78ce783c05d8411b203: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen29650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29651" type="x-p"/> If I go forth into the field, then behold the slain with the sword - Every place presents frightful spectacles; the wounded, the dying, the starving, and the slain; none to bury the dead, none to commiserate the dying, none to bring either relief or consolation. Even the prophets and the priests are obliged to leave the cities, and wander about in unfrequented and unknown places, seeking for the necessaries of life. Dr. Blayney thinks that the going about of the prophets and priests of the land, is to be understood thus: - "They went trafficking about with their false doctrines and lying predictions, as peddlers do with their wares, seeking their own gain." I think the other sense preferable.
entries.e1a0bccc216d804b46374de1e2bd5f1f63daec9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen29651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29652" type="x-p"/> We looked for peace - We expected prosperity when Josiah purged the land of idolatry. <div eID="gen29652" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29653" type="x-p"/> And there is no good - For we have relapsed into our former ways.
entries.84cef9ddd33afa247c18fe65eb1801d8f108c338: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen29653" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29654" type="x-p"/> We acknowledge, O Lord, our wickedness - This the prophet did in behalf of the people; but, alas! they did not join him.
entries.c7b07ff8926e307f5e4441f31ffabf2ce62248bf: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen29654" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29655" type="x-p"/> Do not disgrace the throne of thy glory - The temple. Let not this sacred place be profaned by impious and sacrilegious hands. <div eID="gen29655" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29656" type="x-p"/> Break not thy covenant - See <reference osisRef="Exo.24.7">Exo 24:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exo.24.8">Exo 24:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exo.19.5">Exo 19:5</reference>. They had already broken the covenant, and they wish God to fulfill his part. They ceased to be his people, for they abandoned themselves to idolatry; and yet they wished Jehovah to be their Lord; to defend, support, and fill them with all good things! But when the conditions of a covenant are broken by one of the contracting parties, the other party is not bound; and the covenant is necessarily annulled.
entries.993b822d560c0562b2b6341746f1cbb07ba83b35: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen29656" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29657" type="x-p"/> Are there any among the vanities of the Gentiles - Probably the dearth was now coming, as there had been a long want of rain. It was the prerogative of the true God to give rain and send showers at the prayers of his people. <div eID="gen29657" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen29658" type="x-p"/> Therefore we will wait upon thee - If thou do not undertake for us, we must be utterly ruined.  <chapter eID="Jer.14"/> <div eID="gen29658" type="x-p"/>

entries.3833467bb20a985d5607a534e3944d7b5d3bfd9b: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference> <div eID="gen13995" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> The Uselessness of Prayer on behalf of the People. - The title in <reference osisRef="Jer.14.1">Jer 14:1</reference> specifies the occasion for the following discourse: <hi type="italic">What came a word of Jahveh to Jeremiah concerning the drought.</hi> - Besides here, אשׁר היה is made to precede the דבר יהוה in <reference osisRef="Jer.46.1">Jer 46:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.47.1">Jer 47:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.49.34">Jer 49:34</reference>; and so, by a kind of attraction, the prophecy which follows receivers an outward connection with that which precedes. Concerning the matters of the droughts. בּצּרות, plur. of בּצּרה, <reference osisRef="Ps.9.10">Psa 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.10.1">Psa 10:1</reference>, might mean harassments, troubles in general. But the description of a great drought, with which the prophecy begins, taken along with <reference osisRef="Jer.17.8">Jer 17:8</reference>, where בּצּרת occurs, meaning drought, lit., cutting off, restraint of rain, shows that the plural here is to be referred to the sing. בּצּרת (cf. עשׁתּרות from עשׁתּרת), and that it means the withholding of rain or drought (as freq. in Chald.). We must note the plur., which is not to be taken as intensive of a great drought, but points to repeated droughts. Withdrawal of rain was threatened as a judgment against the despisers of God’s word (Lev 26:19.; <reference osisRef="Deut.11.17">Deu 11:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.28.23">Deu 28:23</reference>); and this chastisement has at various times been inflicted on the sinful people; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.3.3">Jer 3:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.12.4">Jer 12:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.23.10">Jer 23:10</reference>; Hag 1:10. As the occasion of the present prophecy, we have therefore to regard not a single great drought, but a succession of droughts. Hence we cannot fix the time at which the discourse was composed, since we have no historical notices as to the particular times at which God was then punishing His people by withdrawing the rain.
entries.42284434fb0c1814f3e462cebbc15021031d8708: <reference osisRef="Jer.14.2-Jer.14.6">Jer 14:2-6</reference> <hi type="italic">Description of the distress arising from the drought. -</hi> Jer 14:2. <hi type="italic">Judah mourneth, and the gates thereof languish, like mourning on the ground, and the cry of Jerusalem goeth up.</hi> Jer 14:3. <hi type="italic">Their nobles send their mean ones for water: they come to the wells, find no water, return with empty pitchers, are ashamed and confounded and cover their head.</hi> Jer 14:4. <hi type="italic">For the ground, which is confounded, because no rain is fallen upon the earth, the husbandmen are ashamed, cover their head.</hi> Jer 14:5. <hi type="italic">Yea, the hind also in the field, she beareth and forsaketh it, because there is no grass.</hi> Jer 14:6. <hi type="italic">And the wild asses stand on the bare-topped heights, gasp for air like the jackals; their eyes fail because there is no herb."</hi> <div eID="gen13996" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13997" type="x-p"/> The country and the city, the distinguished and the mean, the field and the husbandmen, are thrown into deep mourning, and the beasts of the field pine away because neither grass nor herb grows. This description gives a touching picture of the distress into which the land and its inhabitants have fallen for lack of rain. Judah is the kingdom or the country with its inhabitants; the gates as used poetically for the cities with the citizens. Not mankind only, but the land itself mourns and pines away, with all the creatures that live on it; cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.14.4">Jer 14:4</reference>, where the ground is said to be dismayed along with the tillers of it. The gates of the cities are mentioned as being the places where the citizens congregate. אמלל, fade away, pine, is strengthened by: are black, i.e., mourn, down to the earth; pregnant for: set themselves mourning on the ground. As frequently, Jerusalem is mentioned alongside of Judah as being its capital. Their cry of anguish rises up to heaven. This universal mourning is specialized from <reference osisRef="Jer.14.3">Jer 14:3</reference> on. Their nobles, i.e., the distinguished men of Judah and Jerusalem, send their mean ones, i.e., their retainers or servants and maids, for water to the wells (גּבים, pits, 2Ki 3:16, here cisterns). The <hi type="italic">Chet</hi>. צעור, here and in <reference osisRef="Jer.48.4">Jer 48:4</reference>, is an unusual form for צעיר, <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>. Finding no water, they return, their vessels empty, i.e., with empty pitchers, ashamed of their disappointed hope. בּשׁוּ is strengthened by the synonym הכלמוּ. Covering the head is a token of deep grief turned inwards upon itself; cf. <reference osisRef="2Sam.15.30">2Sa 15:30</reference>; 2Sa 19:5. האדמה is the ground generally. חתּה is a relative clause: <hi type="italic">quae consternata est</hi>. "Because no rain," etc., literally as in 1Ki 17:7. - Even the beasts droop and perish. כּי is intensive: yea, even. The hind brings forth and forsakes, sc. the new-born offspring, because for want of grass she cannot sustain herself and her young. עזוב, <hi type="italic">infin. abs</hi>. set with emphasis for the <hi type="italic">temp. fin</hi>., as <reference osisRef="Gen.41.43">Gen 41:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.8.11">Exo 8:11</reference>, and often; cf. Gesen. §131, 4, <hi type="italic">a</hi>, Ew. §351, <hi type="italic">c</hi>. The hind was regarded by the ancients as tenderly caring for her young, cf. Boch. <hi type="italic">Hieroz</hi>. i. lib. 3, c. 17 (ii. p. 254, ed. Ros.) The wild asses upon the bleak mountain-tops, where these animals choose to dwell, gasp for air, because, by reason of the dreadful drought, it is not possible to get a breath of air even on the hills. Like the תּנּים, jackals, cf. <reference osisRef="Jer.9.10">Jer 9:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.10.22">Jer 10:22</reference>, etc. <hi type="italic">Vulg</hi>. has <hi type="italic">dracones</hi>, with the Aram. versions; and Hitz. and Graf are of opinion that the mention of jackals is not here in point, and that, since תּנּים does not mean <hi type="italic">dracones</hi>, the word stands here, as in <reference osisRef="Exod.29.3">Exo 29:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.32.2">Exo 32:2</reference>, for תּנּין, the monster inhabiting the water, a crocodile or some kind of whale that stretches its head out of the water to draw breath with gaping jaws.
